strengths: AVIS addresses a meaningful gap between audio-visual semantic segmentation and video instance segmentation by requiring identities and sound activity to be tracked together. AVISeg provides a substantial resource: 94,074 masks across 926 videos, 26 categories, and a mean duration of 61.4 seconds. This benchmark has clear potential value for multimodal vision research. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b03/review-experiment-ovokcc99/call-0c8eacba2dc54b84aab2825fb358ec64/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The reported comparisons support the baseline's effectiveness. With common backbone and training settings, AVISM achieves 61.73 HOTA and 40.57 mAP, compared with 57.48/36.25 for VITA and 57.39/37.84 for COMBO (Table 2). The benchmark contribution and consistent improvements on established metrics provide the main basis for weak acceptance.

The architecture is a reasonable adaptation of established segmentation and tracking components. Table 4 supports both audio-fusion stages: HOTA increases from 57.48 without either module to 59.59 with frame-level fusion and 61.73 with both. The architecture diagrams, supplementary implementation details, and explicit same-category failure cases help readers understand the approach and its limitations.
weaknesses: The new FSLA metric has a material specification problem. Algorithm 1 counts silent frames as correct without checking predictions, initializes counters outside the threshold loop without resetting them, and omits explicit object-count equality and the stated class averaging. Its literal implementation cannot explain the varying silent-frame scores in Table 2. This prevents reproduction of an advertised contribution, although it does not establish that the separately reported HOTA/mAP results are wrong. The statement that mAP does not penalize nonsounding predictions is also too broad: false positives can reduce AP depending on confidence ranking.

The conclusions about multimodal large models exceed what the evaluation establishes. Supplement E merges all same-category masks into one identity for Sam4AVS and BuboGPT, and treats each category as one instance for AL-Ref-SAM 2. Sam4AVS also receives only the top-one audio category per segment. These choices structurally prevent successful handling of important AVIS cases. Table 3 demonstrates limitations of these particular adapted pipelines, but cannot isolate the underlying models' instance reasoning or temporal capabilities.

Dataset annotation reliability is insufficiently documented for the central challenge. Section 4 describes SAM-assisted masks and repeated manual review, but provides no measured annotation agreement or error audit, and little guidance for resolving overlapping same-category sources or sound activity within one-second intervals. Source-level separation or duplicate screening across the random video splits is also unspecified. These are gaps in evidence, rather than demonstrated annotation errors or leakage.

Evidence for long-range and same-category reasoning remains limited. Table 5 establishes a window-size/capacity tradeoff, but there are no quantitative breakdowns by video duration, reappearance gap, or simultaneous same-category instances. Figure 10 identifies failures precisely in the latter setting. Sampling at 1 FPS also limits the temporal resolution supported by the evaluation, while maximum-frame counts alone do not establish end-to-end efficiency.

Architectural originality is modest: object-token compression, shifted-window processing, and matching/similarity losses largely follow Mask2Former and VITA. The strongest novelty therefore lies in the task and dataset. Smaller reproducibility issues include unspecified training clip sampling and fusion-layer depth; these reporting omissions are less consequential than the metric and evaluation concerns above.
